intros.market: The certificate market remains highly concentrated, with the top five CAs controlling 88% of issuance. Internet Security Research Group leads at 32%, followed by Google Trust Services at 21.1% and DigiCert at 17.8%. The CR3 ratio of 70.92% and HHI of 1980 indicate moderate concentration, though 74 of 88 trusted CAs operate in the long tail with minimal market share.
intros.trust: Browser trust stores disagree substantially on which certificate authorities to trust, with 335 total roots distributed across four major programs but only 90 roots trusted by all four stores. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating the largest source of store divergence. Only 38 CA owners appear in all four stores, forcing certificate subscribers to navigate a fragmented trust landscape where a valid chain in Edge may fail in Chrome.
intros.conc: Three CAs issue more than 70% of all trusted certificates, creating systemic dependency on Internet Security Research Group, Google Trust Services, and DigiCert. An HHI of 1980 signals moderate market concentration, but the 88% top-5 share reveals practical consolidation around a handful of providers. Any operational failure or distrust action against a top-3 CA would immediately affect the majority of HTTPS-enabled websites.
intros.tail: Seventy-four certificate authorities hold full trust store inclusion despite issuing a combined 12% of certificates, creating asymmetric risk exposure for browsers and relying parties. These long-tail CAs face the same complex compliance obligations as high-volume issuers but operate with less public scrutiny and fewer resources. The gap between trust store presence and operational maturity becomes apparent in incident data, where 55 CAs have disclosed at least one compliance failure.
intros.geo: United States-based CAs issue 92.73% of all trusted certificates despite representing only 15 of 88 trusted authorities. European CAs account for 44 entities but generate just 7.18% of issuance, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively produce 0.09%. This geographic concentration ties global certificate infrastructure to US legal jurisdiction and regulatory frameworks, amplifying the impact of US-based policy decisions.
intros.gov: Thirty state-operated or state-owned certificate authorities hold trust store inclusion, though they collectively issue only 0.09% of certificates. These government CAs span multiple regions and represent diverse national interests, creating potential vectors for state-level surveillance or compelled access. Their presence in browser trust stores grants sovereign entities the technical capability to intercept HTTPS traffic within their jurisdictions, independent of their actual issuance volume.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions present high legal risk for certificate authority operations due to broad surveillance authorities or compelled disclosure frameworks, including China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk under current legal assessment. These classifications intersect with the 30 government-operated CAs in trust stores, where state ownership and legal jurisdiction compound to create elevated interception risk regardless of public issuance volume.
intros.ops: Certificate authorities have disclosed 1,734 compliance incidents across 55 organizations, with misissuance accounting for 668 cases and governance failures for 558. CAs self-report only 31% of incidents, while 18% come from external security researchers and 15% from automated scanning tools, revealing gaps in internal detection capabilities. Root program oversight identified just 4% of incidents directly, though 238 incidents involved explicit policy failures and 159 involved disclosure violations.
intros.crypto: The cryptographic posture data for 2026 is not included in the current digest, preventing analysis of root algorithm distribution, key size compliance, or cryptographic agility across the trusted CA population. This gap limits visibility into preparation for post-quantum transitions and adherence to current algorithm deprecation schedules.
intros.distrust: Browsers have executed 16 distrust actions against certificate authorities, with 14 cases citing compliance or operational failures and 10 involving patterns of repeated issues. Seven CAs exhibited negligent noncompliance, three demonstrated willful circumvention of requirements, and three showed demonstrated incompetence in their operational posture. The median runway from distrust announcement to effective date spans 1,185 days, offering substantial time for certificate replacement but also prolonging exposure to untrusted issuers.
intros.policy: Active TLS-issuing CAs show mixed readiness for staged validity reductions under Ballot SC-081, with 5 of 35 CAs still issuing certificates near the 100-day threshold as the March 2027 deadline approaches and only 9 consistently operating at the 47-day target required by March 2029. This operational adjustment occurs against a compliance surface that has grown 121x since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations spanning CA/B Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and supporting IETF/NIST standards. Seventy-six percent of these obligations carry mandatory compliance language, yet no new ballots have passed since 2022 despite continued regulatory expansion.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has declined sharply from 2019 levels, with Chrome reviewing just 18.4% of 223 incidents in 2025 compared to 67.8% coverage in 2019. Mozilla coverage dropped from 78.0% to 9.9% over the same period, while Apple addressed only 5.4% of incidents and Microsoft provided zero substantive oversight. Chrome has participated in 740 total oversight bugs with 115 substantive actions recently, but the dropping coverage rate suggests stretched resources relative to the 1,734 total incidents disclosed across the ecosystem.
intros.community: Twenty-one of 56 CA/B Forum members actively contribute to ballot development, while 35 maintain zero-contribution status despite holding voting rights. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual ballot activity with 36 proposals and 1 endorsement, and Sectigo ranks as the most active organizational participant overall. This concentration of policy development among a small subset of members means governance decisions rest with the same entities appearing in market share and incident data.
intros.audit: Independent auditors caught just 27% of in-scope compliance incidents that later appeared in public bug reports, indicating that clean audit letters frequently coexist with real operational failures. Forty-one CAs show high transparency gaps between audit statements and disclosed incidents, while only 6 received qualified opinions despite widespread compliance issues. WebTrust self-reporting reaches 62.9% and ETSI self-reporting 69.5%, but only 12 CAs have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, and 6 CAs changed auditors in 2025 amid scrutiny of audit quality.
